utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Monday, the 15th of March, 2010. I would, first of all, like to greet the accused who are present in the courtroom. I have noted that Mr. Pusic and Mr. Praljak are not present. I would like to greet Defence counsel, all the representatives of the OTP, as well as all the people assisting us. I believe that the Registrar has an IC number to give us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Coric Defence has submitted their list of documents tendered through Witness Miroslav Desnica. This list shall be given Exhibit IC01202. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. We shall bring the witness into the courtroom. But before that, I need to hand down an oral decision which I shall read out slowly. Oral decision ordering the Petkovic Defence a dead-line to file a written submission on the admission of evidence pursuant to Guide-line 9 of the decision of the 24th of April, 2008. At the hearing of 11th of March, 2010, the Petkovic Defence stated, having finished the presentation of its case, and asked whether the Trial Chamber could specify on what date the filing of a request to admit the evidence. It is a decision of 8th of February, 2010. The Trial Chamber had already asked the Petkovic Defence to disclose, in the shortest time possible, a date on which it may perhaps file a written motion pursuant to Guide-line 9 of decision rendered on the 24th of April, 2008. In this oral decision, the Trial Chamber emphasised the fact that whatever the case may be, these motions needed to be filed before the end of the presentation of the Petkovic Defence's case. At the hearing of 17th of February, 2010, the Petkovic Defence had told the Trial Chamber that it would file such a written motion on the last day of Milivoj Petkovic's testimony, i.e., at the time on the 1st of March, 2010, or that it would request an extension of the dead-line to file such a motion. In light of the dead-lines imposed by the Trial Chamber in its oral decision of 8th of February, 2010, the Trial Chamber holds that this application, filed by the Petkovic Defence, arrived rather late in time and should have been filed before the end of its case. Therefore, the Trial Chamber holds that only a short dead-line may be granted to the Petkovic Defence to file a written motion pursuant to Guide-line 9 and, therefore, orders the Petkovic Defence to file such a motion by the 22nd of March, 2010, at the latest. In short, the Petkovic Defence must file its motion by the 22nd of March, 2010, to admit its evidence pursuant to Guide-line 9. Have you understood, Ms. Alaburic?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good afternoon. Of course, I understand your decision, and we will be filing a motion by that date. I thought that it was understood that we asked for a fortnight from the time that the Petkovic Defence case ends, and I apologise if there was a misunderstanding. But, yes, that time, a week, will be sufficient. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Andabak, could you stand up, please. Could you give me your first name, last name, and date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am Zdenko Andabak, born on the 21st of November, 1968, in Livno.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your occupation currently, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a retired colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, have you already testified before a court of law, or is it the first time that you're testifying today, on those facts that took place in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've never testified before. This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please read the text of the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, Colonel, you may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, just some information I'd like to share with you. You are a witness of Mr. Valentin Coric's Defence. You will be answering questions which will be put to you in a moment by Ms. Tomic, who is Mr. Coric's lawyer, and she will show you documents contained in the binder which you should have or which you will be given a little later. Once those questions are finished, the other Defence counsel may then also put questions to you as part of time allotted to them already, and the Prosecutor, who's sitting on your right-hand side, will have two hours to cross-examine you. If need be, Ms. Tomic will be entitled to put extra questions to you. The three Judges sitting before you - we are four Judges normally; that is not the case today - may at any time put questions to you. Usually, these are questions designed to clarify the contents of those documents we have before us. Try and be as accurate as you possibly can when you answer. If there is a question you don't understand, please don't hesitate to ask the person who has put it to you to rephrase it, even if it is a Judge. You are now a witness of the Court, since you have taken the solemn declaration. You will be testifying until Thursday. That said, there will be no hearing tomorrow. Until Thursday, you must not contact Mr. Valentin Coric's Defence. We have a break -- a 20-minute break every hour and a half so that you can have a break and that we can change our tapes. If for any particular reason you wish to stop, raise your hand and we will then have a break. You will soon realise that it is extremely exhausting to answer questions at length by questions put to you by counsel, Prosecutors and Judges. So far, everyone has managed to cope with this without any problems whatsoever, which I hope you will be able to do also. This is what I wanted to share with you so that this hearing unfolds in the best conditions possible. We all have the establishment of the truth in mind. Ms. Coric [as interpreted], you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to you too, Mr. Andabak.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May the witness be provided with the binder and the documents. And with the Trial Chamber's permission, I'd like to ask some leading questions to begin with - the Prosecution does not object - linked to the witness's career in the HVO and afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, I'm going to read out a brief CV listing your positions in the HVO. And having done that, I'm going to ask you whether that is correct. In May 1992, you became commander of a company of the military police, attached to the Brigade of the Municipal Staff of the HVO of Livno, and you remained in that post until the 1st of July, 1992, when you became commander of the military police in the operative group called North-East Herzegovina. And you remained in that post until the 25th of November, 1992, when you became commander of the 2nd Battalion of the Military Police, staying in that position until 1993, when you became chief of the traffic police -- general and traffic police. And you remained in that post until the 28th of June, 1993, when you became assistant head of the Military Police Administration for the North-East Herzegovina Operative Zone. And you remained in that post until the end of November 1993, when you once again became commander of the 2nd Military Police Battalion. In March 1994, you were appointed chief of the general military police in the Military Police Administration of the HVO, and from the military police of the HVO you left on the 30th of June, 1994, to join the MUP, and you remained there until 2001, when you joined the Armed Forces of the Army of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the Command for Training and Doctrine. And you remained there until November 2007, when you retired with the rank of colonel in the Armed Forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, from the post of commander, the Centre for Combat Simulation, attached to the Command for Training and Doctrine in Banja Luka. Is that all correct? Everything that I've read out, is it correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, everything that you've just read out is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: To start off with now, linked to your CV, I would like us to look at a few documents, and they are in the order in which I shall be asking you about them. I'm going to ask you whether the documents refer to your CV and the various appointments that we just listed. In order to do that, look at PD02164 [as interpreted] first, please. 5D is the number, 5D2164, 02164. The next document is P00803 and then P01460, P02230, P02963, P02996, and, finally, 5D05084. Mr. Andabak, are those all documents which relate to the biographical data I presented earlier on?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, those are the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Tell us now, please, Mr. Andabak, in 1992 did a provision exist regulating the military police organisation, control and command of the military police, and the remit and tasks of the military police?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: As far as I remember, from April 1992 there were rules and regulations governing the establishment of the military police, signed by the president, Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Now look at the document P00143, please. Have you found the document?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Will you tell the Court what document this is? What is it?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: It is provisional instructions for the work of the military police units of the Croatian Defence Council in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and they are instructions for the work of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Andabak, were you acquainted with these instructions?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, I was, and so were the officers from the military police subordinate to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Andabak, according to these instructions, how was the military police organised?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: In April 1992, the military police was organised on the basis of municipal staffs of the HVO, which meant that members of the military police were within the local brigades and their headquarters acting in a given area.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Now, with these instructions, did they regulate the relationships between the Military Police Administration and the military police on the ground?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, these instructions did regulate that relationship, and the military police had the duty of waging cadres policy on the ground; that is to say, appointments, dismissals, disciplinary measures, and so on and so forth. And it was there to see to the equipment, and uniforms, and professional training for the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Andabak, in that year, 1992, how was command of the military police regulated? Who commanded the military police, in actual fact? Who was in command? Who was your commander?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: At that time in 1992, command of the military police was carried out through the brigade command in the area where the military police was active.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, take a look at the next document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please, Colonel. Your answer lies at the heart of the issue here, the police and the military brigade. I would like you to look at number 4 of the document we have before us on page 0040 [as interpreted], 737 in the English version. Let me state the number again, 40, 737, 737. Look at number 4. In the English as we have it on the screen, it begins with: "All military police units ...," under item 4. And in your language, I would be incapable of telling you what it says. It must be, I believe, under item 4 also in your language. What does this mean, this here? What is the exact meaning of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This means that the commander -- a commander of an OG is also in command of the military police, in operative terms, in the field. Since military police units were attached to the brigades of the municipal headquarters of the HVO, that means that the OG commander was the factual commander of the military police. But at that moment, the military police units in the field were subordinate to the brigades.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are saying that the military police is subordinated to the brigade; is that right? That is on line 21 of page 9. That was my question for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, in order to clarify the meaning of "operative command," tell us, please, whether that means operative command in combat or in general terms. What is the precise explanation for the term "operative command"?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: "Operative command" means to carry out all daily policing jobs, extraordinary tasks, and combat tasks in an area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: And now please look at the following document, which is P008 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. I think if we want to be complete, we should also look at paragraph 5, the next one, in the same document, which says, and I quote: "The commanders of smaller units shall be held responsible for their work and for carrying out their tasks to the commander of the military police battalion, who, in turn, shall be responsible to the Military Police Administration." If one looks at these two, one gets the impression that there is a double chain of responsibility, one within the military command that would go up to the supreme military commander, and the other one to the Military Police Administration, and I think it would be helpful if you could explain to the Chamber the difference, what characterises one or the other. Now, it is possible, Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic, that you have this question somewhere in your list, and in that case I would just have it on record and wait until it fits into your plan. I see that you are nodding. So, Witness, you are at this moment relieved of answering my question, because it will come from your counsel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't see an obstacle for the witness to answer. It was very much in line with our plan, anyway, so he can explain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is true that commanders were subordinated to the units of the military police, in my operative zone were responsible to me and answerable to me, but I, in turn, was answerable to -- for reporting to the Administration of the Military Police by means of daily report and inform them about the activities of the military police in my field, i.e., in the field of the OG.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I let you go on, Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic, because you're probably aware of the fact that this does not exhaust the problem, but I do not want to interfere excessively with your own work.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now let's look at P00837.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this document? This is another instruction for the work of military police units, dating back to the month of November 1992. Are you acquainted with this document?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with the instructions.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, when it comes to this instruction, did anything change, in practical terms, in the field, in terms of the organisation and command and control of the military police?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: No, as a matter of fact, nothing changed. The military police companies were united, but in terms of the system of control and command, nothing changed. The administration still had the same authorities and competencies, and I, as the commander of that military -- of that battalion, was subordinated to the military commander in the area where I was active.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, you've just told us about operative command, and you said that your operative commander was the commander of the OG or the operative zone. Did you also receive orders from the Military Police administration, and if you did, what kind of orders those were?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: We received orders from the Military Police Administration as well. Those were in form of regulations and instructions about, for example, blockades or, for example, if we were to carry out an escort duty for military vehicles or transports, if we were to protect foreign officials, and if that was to be done by the military police, those were the kind of orders we received, but those were very few and far between.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, who did you report to about your work? Who were you answerable to you, in practical terms, in the field? Could you describe the situation for us?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: I was the commander of the 2nd Battalion of the Military Police in the North-West Herzegovina OG, and I was under the command of the OG North-West Herzegovina or, rather, OZ, not Herzegovina, whose commander was Zeljko Siljeg, headquartered in Tomislavgrad.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: I'm going to give you an example. For example, you refused to carry out Mr. Siljeg's order, you don't carry that order out, or you do something which you are not supposed to do or you're not allowed to do. What will happen to you? Whose duty will it be to deal with your omission or your breach of discipline?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: The commander of the operations zone will certainly file the report against me to the Main Staff, and then the Main Staff will inform the Military Police Administration, because the Military Police Administration appointed me as a battalion commander, and there will probably be disciplinary proceedings against me or a criminal report if I committed a crime. So it will be either the commander of the operative zone or his assistant for security.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Andabak, let's look at the following document. And while you are looking for it, let me say that this is P00957. Have you got it?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: And can you describe the document for us?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, I've got the document, and the document is the organisation of the HVO in late 1992, and that was in effect as of the 1st of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, according to this organisation scheme, how was the military police of the HVO organised and how was the situation on the ground, in factual terms?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: According to that organisation, in addition to the Military Police Administration there were also five military police battalions of which the first one was an active battalion, and it was under the direct command of the Military Police Administration. A novelty in this organisation was that that battalion was active in the entire territory of the HZ-HB.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: What does it mean when you say that it was under the direct command of the Military Police Administration?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: That means that the chief of the Military Police Administration could send that battalion to any region pursuant to an order of the Main Staff of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, when that first active battalion arrived in a region pursuant to such an order, who was its commander, under whose command was it?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: If that first active battalion was to report to the OZ North-West Herzegovina, the commander of the 1st Battalion, pursuant to that order, would report to me. I would be responsible to receive that battalion, and the orders and sending them to carry out a regular task or a combat task was something that the commander of the OZ North-West Herzegovina would give them if they arrived in our territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Andabak, let's look at the second page in the Croatian version. In English, it's also page 2, towards the bottom of the page. At the beginning of the second page, if you look at it, you will see reference made to the 2nd Battalion, headquartered in Tomislavgrad, and covering the OZ North-West Herzegovina. Would that be the battalion that you have just been telling us about and whose commander you were?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's the battalion, but its headquarters were not in Tomislavgrad but in Livno. That was the change that was effected. And Livno is also in that same OZ.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, how was your battalion made up? What did it consist of?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: My battalion was made up of the Command, the Crime Department, the Communications Department, and three detachments of the military police, and also Operative Duty Service.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, I can see here in the first sentence a reference being made to six brigade platoons of the military police, and somewhat further down in this same paragraph it says that there are six independent brigade platoons of the military police in the battalion. They were also on the strength of the brigades in the North-West Herzegovina OZ. Could you please explain to the Trial Chamber how come that it says first that they were on your strength and then later on it says that they were on the strength of the brigades? Can you explain that for us and tell us how it actually was in the field?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Since the organisation applied to the whole strength of the military police, and those six brigade platoons were deployed in the OZ, where the 2nd Battalion of the Military Police was also deployed, that's why they are listed here. The 2nd Battalion of the Military Police had nothing whatsoever to do with the brigade platoons. And as you will see further on, they were on the strength of their respective brigades and they were responsible to them and answerable for them for their work.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, in 1993, after this organisation came into effect, who was your operative commander?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: As I have already said it before, I'm repeating it again. My operative commander was the OZ North-West Herzegovina, where I was deployed and where I was active.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the following document, Mr. Andabak, which is P00960. The title of the document is "Instructions on the Implementation of the New Organisational Scheme of the Military Police Units." The document was issued in December 1992. On page 2 in the Croatian version, and also in the English version, it says that: "We propose that commissions be set up consisting of the following members, for the purpose of the reorganisation of VP units." And then it says for the battalions, the president of the commission, the commander, and other members are mentioned; the commander of the OZ, an officer from the Military Police Administration. And a few paragraphs later, it says that the appointment of officers and commanders shall be carried out in keeping with the decision on the internal organisation of the Defence Department after the 10th of January, 1993. Until that moment, commissions from each OZ have to submit their co-ordinated proposals for the command and officers' positions in the OZ. Tell me, Mr. Andabak -- we see that the commander of the military police battalion is mentioned as the chairman of the commission, and you say that you were the commander of the MP battalion. Do you remember this, and was this ever implemented, the instructions that we have just read out in this document?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: I remember this document. This was implemented as is stated in the order.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: And now let's look at the following document in your binder, which is PD00538 [as interpreted] -- 5D00538. These are the minutes from the co-ordination with the commanders in the North-West Herzegovina OZ, dated 9th of March, 1993. Mr. Andabak, were you present during this co-ordination meeting, and in what capacity, if you were?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: I attended the meeting in the OZ in Tomislavgrad as the chief of general and traffic police, which means that I represented the MP Administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what you discussed at the meeting and why you attended the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: As can be seen from the document, the first item was organisation and tasks of the military police, and the commander of the operative zone wanted to take advantage of this opportunity to inform all the commanders that he was in command of any OZ about the establishment of the military police, its organisation, from the beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Fine, Mr. Andabak. We can move on to the next document, which is P03000. This is a document entitled "Information" about changes in the military police establishment, dated the 28th of June, 1993. Tell me whether you knew about these changes in establishment and organisation? And if so, what changes took place?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: I did know about this organisation and notification. As the result of the escalation of the Croatian-Bosnian conflict, light assault brigades were established, battalions, for each operative zone in the HZ-HB. And in addition to the light assault battalions, we also had the active-duty military police battalions working in the individual zones. And another innovation was that assistant commanders, or, rather, heads of the military police commanders for the operative zones were appointed.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Andabak, it says here -- well, when I read out your CV, as far as I remember, you were assistant head of the -- assistant head at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: It says here, at the end of that page: "Joining up the military police activities of the light assault battalion and the BP Battalion within the corresponding operations zone shall be conducted by the assistant head of the Military Police Administration responsible for that zone, who is also authorised to command the battalions." Tell us what that means. What was your job as assistant chief?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: I was a co-ordinator between the 2nd Light Assault Military Police Battalion and the 6th Battalion, when it came to commanding, so I was -- the commander of the operative zone issued assignments to me for the military police in the operative zone, and I would convey this to the light assault battalion, pass it on, and the command of the 6th Light Assault Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Andabak, as commander of a battalion, throughout your career in the military police did you attend any meetings at the level of the Military Police Administration?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Well, according to our monthly plan and programme, we had one meeting a month with the Military Police Administration, that is to say, the chief of the Military Police Administration, and the chief of the General and Traffic Department, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: And what would you discuss at those meetings?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: We mostly analysed reports from the previous month and decided upon the activities we would undertake in the forthcoming period, with the conclusions made -- that is to say, we made conclusions as to who would do what. And among other things, we also discussed the problem of the military -- the problems that the military police encountered on the ground. We discussed logistics for the military police, care of the wounded members of the military police, as well as assistance to families of killed policemen.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Would you now take a look at document P08 -- P0869 [as interpreted], and tell the Court -- P05869 is the document number. Could you tell the Court what document this is, just briefly? Do you recognise it, and what is it about?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: I recognise the document. It's an excerpt from the minutes of one of our monthly meetings, regular monthly meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now look at the next document, which is P04947, and I'm going to ask you the same question. Are you familiar and do you recognise this document? Do you know what it's about?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, it's the same document with another date or, rather, a meeting held in a different month.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Andabak. Let's move on to the next document. P00781 is the number, and this is a document from the commander of the Operative Zone of North-West Herzegovina. It is a report on the establishment of commands for the North-East Herzegovina Operative Zone. It says here that within the establishment system of the North-West Herzegovina area, the following units are included. And under number 9, it says: "The 2nd Military Police Battalion - Livno." Tell us, Mr. Andabak, the 2nd Military Police Battalion of Livno, was it within the establishment of this or not? And if it was, what does that mean, that it was part of the establishment or organisation?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, the 2nd Military Police Battalion in the operative zone was within the composition of the operative zone, as it says here. And as I've already said before, I was re-subordinated to the commander of the operative zone in carrying out my tasks and assignments.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, a few minutes ago you told us that the brigade platoons of the military police were within the composition of the brigades. Tell us now, please, who appointed commanders to the brigade platoons of the military police in your operative zone?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: In North-West Herzegovina's operative zone, the commanders for the brigade military police was appointed -- were appointed by the commander of the brigade, and he could also dismiss them if they failed to carry out their assignments.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Did you, yourself, appoint anyone from the Military Police Administration?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel repeat that question, please? Could counsel repeat her question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: The translators ask you to repeat your questions, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: My question was as follows, and I repeat: Did you, or anybody else from the Military Police Administration, appoint a commander of a platoon belonging to the brigade military police in the Operative Zone of North-West Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't, I didn't appoint anyone, and I also know that the Military Police Administration didn't appoint commanders of the brigade military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Andabak, would you take a look at document P0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, I look at this document, P00781. The good thing about this document is that we can see that the 2nd Military Police Battalion reports to the commander of the operative zone; namely, Colonel Siljeg. This is written in black and white. I will give you an example just for argument's sake. If Colonel Siljeg told you that you had to strengthen the Eugen Kvaternik Brigade in Bugojno, would you abide by this order or would you ask Valentin Coric for his authorisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, from other organisational units of the military police which are located in the OZ of North-West Herzegovina, but under my command, I would have appointed a platoon or company, depending on what I had been ordered by the commander of the OZ, and I would send that unit to the Eugen Kvaternik Brigade to carry out its tasks, and they there would be under the command of the commander of the Eugen Kvaternik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you're saying that you would have appointed a platoon or a company to strengthen the Eugen Kvaternik Brigade. But while taking this decision, would you have, yourself, asked Valentin Coric for his green light or his authorisation, or could you decide on your own accord? Was it part of your own competences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would inform in writing Mr. Coric about the deployment of the military police. But since the military police battalion has its platoons and companies within the operative zone, it wasn't necessary for us to be given reinforcements based on an order from Valentin Coric, except if another military police unit was coming in with -- or, rather, from another operative zone. Then, via the Main Staff, Valentin Coric would receive an order to send the military police to another operative zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. One last question. You decide to send a company to Bugojno in order to strengthen the Eugen Kvaternik Brigade. Once this company arrives in Bugojno, will it be under the exclusive and total command and the commander of the Eugen Kvaternik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it would be under the command of the brigade, which would then issue it its tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, look at the next document, P04413. It's a warning signed by Mr. Govorusic. Tell me, first, do you know who Mr. Govorusic was and what position he held in August of 1993, when he issued this warning?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Mr. Ante Govorusic was the deputy commander of the OZ of North-West Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did the you take on board this warning?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, we did receive this warning.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: In this warning, it says that it follows a warning from the Main Staff, and it says that the brigade military police, under direct command of the brigade commanders, that it exists in the brigade's formations and has the status just as other brigade units. It says that the selection of men is carried out from the military composition of the brigade and that it is the commander's right to replace any military policeman. And then it goes on to say that the chief of the military police can be asked for professional assistance. And it goes on to say that the problems in the brigade police are resolved through the system of control and command. Now, Mr. Andabak, you've already told us something about this, but were you aware of the functioning of the brigade military police in this way, and is that how it functioned in the North-West Herzegovina OZ?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: The brigade military police was under the direct command of the brigade commander, and that was what it was like in the North-West Herzegovina OZ, and the men -- the manpower was also from the brigade. And as far as the Military Police Administration is concerned, it was duty-bound, logistically, to ensure military police equipment and professional training for brigade military policemen. In item 3 here, it says that the chief of the military police can only be asked -- can be asked only for professional assistance, which means that if they needed some rules and regulations governing their work at the entrance gate, for example, or rules and regulations about the various check-points manned by three men, well, that's the kind of professional assistance that was being sought.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who and in what way asked for professional assistance? And do you know of any such cases, in practice, when professional assistance was requested? And if so, what happened?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Professional assistance was sought by the brigade commander, either through the OZ commander or through me, as the battalion commander. It usually went through the commander of the operative zone.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Andabak, let's skip the next document and go to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, on the basis of this document, once again, because in a few months' time this trial will be finished, so we must really be clear about the documents. If the commander of the Kresimir IV Brigade says or tells his company of military policemen that they will not control the check-points because there is no point in that, however, You must place yourselves on the front-line because I need you there, that is where you will be much more useful, at that point in time you, as the commander of the battalion, can you object to that or does that -- is that solely part of the remit of the commander of the Kresimir IV Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that was within the remit of the Petar Kresimir IV Brigade, and he was in command of the brigade military police. In case he issued such an order, he could request from the commander of the operative zone -- if he needed military police for the check-points, he could request assistance from the active battalion of the military police and ask them to control the check-points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that the reason why, in small (a) in this document, which stems from Ante Govorusic, it states that the military police has the same status as the other units of the brigade? Is that why that one gives reason to believe that there is only one chain of command and the person who exercises the supreme authority at the level of the brigade is a brigade commander? Is that why it says here that these units have the same status as the other units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's correct. The military platoon -- the brigade platoon of the military police was on the strength of brigade, and it had enjoyed the same status as the other platoons of the same brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Tomic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I'm skipping a document, and let's look at P00900 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: While you're looking for the document, what you have just told us about the North-West Herzegovina OZ and the command and the status of the military police, according to what you know, did it function in the same way in the other operative zones? P00900 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: All operative zones in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna acted in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Very well. The following document is P00990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The transcript lists the document as "P00900." That's what you've said. Isn't it the document P00990? I see you are nodding. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, and I corrected myself on page 26, line 1, but it was being recorded just as you were the putting your question about the document. So, yes, it is the document, P00990.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: This is an order issued by the brigade commander. The brigade is Stjepan Radic. Tell me, please, where was the Stjepan Radic Brigade deployed, in which operative zone?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: The aforementioned brigade was within the Operative Zone of South-East Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Andabak. We are moving very slowly. I did ask you before your testimony to make breaks, but your breaks are a bit too long. Please count to 10 after I've finished and then start answering. Usually, we have a problem with the breaks being too short, and now they are too long. And now could you please look at the order, and could you please provide your short comment with regard to what has been discussed so far?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: This order was issued by the brigade commander in 1993. As far as I can see, the order was created in the North-West Herzegovina Operations Zone IZM or Forward Command Post Pidris. The brigade commander here acted pursuant to his authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Andabak. Can we please look at the following document, which is P01099. This is a schematic of the brigade organisation, and you will see the schematic on page 2 of the document. Could you please tell us -- I have actually two questions about the schematic. The first question is this: Does the schematic reflect the situation as you knew it at the time with regard to the composition of the brigades in your operations zone? That's my first question. And the second question is this: What's the Protection Platoon's purpose, and what is the purpose of the MP Platoon? What are their roles?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: The document reflects the organisation structure of the brigade and its establishment. The MP Platoon is here to provide security for the brigade command, to control the entry and exit points in the battle-field, to bring back deserters pursuant to the commander's orders, whereas the Protection Platoon acts in combat and moves with the commander and his headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: And now, Mr. Andabak, could you just briefly look at that table which follows, actually the following few pages, and could you please tell us what the table represents?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: This table, as far as I can see, shows the personnel composition in the brigade, and here I can see the command and the headquarters of the brigade with their personnels.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, in the table that we are looking at there are no platoons, battalions, detachments, that we were able to see in the previous schematic. How come? Why are they missing?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: This is probably just an excerpt showing just the command and the headquarters and no affiliated units. This is just an excerpt from the overall organisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me what affiliated units are? We have five battalions here, we have the Signals Platoon, the Reconnaissance Platoon, the MP Platoon. What are affiliated units? Are you saying that they are not on the strength of the brigade or what?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: They were on the strength of the brigade. They were its elements.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: And now look at P04293.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may just ask a question as to this list of persons. To me, it looks like these persons being the members of the staff, full stop, whereas the platoon is an instrument of the staff. The platoon is not a member of the staff, but an instrument used by the staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, here you see the commander and his staff, but if you look at the detail, then you could see the elaboration of the personnel, the platoons, how many men, ranks, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It looks a bit strange. The commander, one person, would have 380 vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would not be able to comment the figures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Would you agree that this table is not entirely convincing as a document, at least not self-evident, as you, yourself, seem to have doubts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, when it comes to logistics and the number of vehicles, yes, it's a bit strange, but the rest is all okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that there has been a mistake in the interpretation of your answer. To clarify things, I'll put the question again.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: You said if we were to look at the details, this table does not contain personnel, platoons, if I understood you properly. Did I understand properly what you were saying?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Battalions -- battalions are divided into the command, the detachment platoons, so if all that was listed, you would also see the number of personnel, officers, non-commissioned officers, civilians working in the battalion, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at the following document, which is P04293. This document was issued by the South-East Herzegovina Operations Zone in August 1993. Its title is "Report on the Organisation and Activities of the Headquarters Office of the 2nd HVO Brigade," and it says here the brigade was not in a position to secure the necessary MTS for the work of the office. And then a few lines further down: "... in order to be able to supply the following units and services in the brigade:" And then the four battalions are listed: The Operations and Training Department, Artillery, Brigade Military Police, Protection Platoon, Logistics Platoon. Tell me, please, Mr. Andabak, what would be your comment on what we have just read? According to what you know, did brigades in your OZ have the same units and services on their strengths?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, every brigade in my OZ had the same organisation and the same units and elements.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I should move to a big, somewhat larger topic, so I would kindly ask you if we could have a break now five minutes before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have our 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, let's look at the following document, P04103. The document again was signed by Mr. Govorusic, the deputy commander of the operative zone, and it is -- it was issued in August 1993. The title is "Report on the Situation in Brigades - Report." Please look at the third page of the document in Croatian, and in English it's on page 6. The title is "The 6th Battalion of the Military Police." Mr. Andabak, was that the battalion of the military police under your command?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, that was the 6th Battalion of the Military Police.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Below the title, it says: "The check on the implementation of the order ..." And further on you can read that the check refers to the number, reporting, work. Do you remember that this check was, indeed, performed, that it was carried out?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, the check did happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now let's look at the following document, which is P04110. And while we're looking for the document, tell me, please, in the your zone did you receive reports from companies and platoons that were on the strength of your battalion?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, we received daily operative reports from them.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Did you also receive reports from the brigade platoons of the military police in your zone?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: When it comes to the brigade platoons of the military police, we did not receive reports from them because they were not duty-bound to report to us, but to the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Now you have the document before you. We can see that this is a document issued by the brigade military police platoon, sent to the command of the brigade, just like you've told us. Could you please look -- somewhere in the middle of the document, it says "BVP." Does this refer to the brigade military police? Does this stand for the brigade military police?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, this is the abbreviation for the brigade military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: It says here BVP was sent to the place where nine dead bodies of Muslim civilians were found. The case was referred to the brigade SIS. Do you know something about the case that is mentioned in here?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: The brigade military police received a report that in a village there were several dead bodies to be found. They went there. They secured the site, and they called the SIS of their own brigade as well as the Crime Prevention Department of the active military police battalion, which took the case over. They carried out an on-site inspection, filed a criminal report. And as far as I know, the perpetrator of that particular crime is still serving sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you know where that was? What is the village in question? You did mention that it was in the village, but what village was that?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: The name of the village was Mokronoge in Tomislavgrad municipality, and the case file name is Bakovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Then we can skip a document and we can move on to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second, Colonel. I'm interested in the fact that nine Muslim civilians were found dead, and you're saying -- or, rather, in this document it says that the case was referred to the SIS. So here is what I would like to know: Why did the military police not carry out this investigation? Why was this case referred to the SIS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, it was the brigade military police which did not have the Crime Prevention Department of the military police, it only existed within the 6th Battalion of the active military police, and that is why they could not carry out an on-site inspection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, could you please look at P00970. And while this is being brought up, I'm going to ask you this: Who did you sent your reports to and what kind of reports those were?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: I, as the commander of the 2nd Battalion of the Military Police, was duty-bound to send daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly, as well as interim reports to the Operative Duty Service of the Military Police Administration and the command of the OZ.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, when a report of yours arrived at the Duty Operations Service of the MP Administration, what happened to it next?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: The officer on duty who received my report, and the reports of the other military commanders from the other OZs, collects them all together, looks at all the items, send on what is interesting for the Military Police Administration and its subordinate units, whether they be the traffic police unit or the general police, crime police, assistant chief of SIS in the Military Police Administration or whatever, and so when they collect all these reports, they send them to the chief of the Military Police Administration. And as far as I know, when he received a report of that kind, he would send it on to the head of the Office of the Main Staff, SIS assistant, Ministry of Defence, and various addressees.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Andabak, your report, did it contain information about what the brigade military police did in your zone?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Since they do not submit reports to me, my reports didn't contain those elements either.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know what it was like in other zones with the reports of other military police?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Well, all I can tell you is what I heard; that is to say, that there were cases in the Operative Zone of South-East Herzegovina whereby military policemen step outside the frameworks of the brigade, and then the commander of the battalion would write such a report to the military police and the duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, would you now look at the document before you now? P00970 is the document - we called it up earlier on - and tell the Court what is this document?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: This is a quarterly report on the work of the 2nd Battalion of the Military Police for North-West Herzegovina OZ.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Is that one of your reports?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, it is, it's my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Who did you send it to? Who were you reporting to?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: As you can see from the heading and title, one copy went to the military police, to the duty officer, and the second to the command of the Operative Zone of North-West Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, in the Croatian version of the document we see something written in hand -- by hand, something handwritten. Do you recognise the writing, whose handwriting that is?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, it's the handwriting of the commander of the operative zone, Mr. Zeljko Siljeg.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, who -- well, let me you this first: As a member of the military police, as a commander of a battalion, did you take part in any combat operations, have any combat assignments?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, I did take part in combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: And, tell me, who did you submit your combat reports to?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: I submitted my combat reports to the commander of the operative zone at the briefings, I reported to him at the briefings.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: And when were these briefings held, who attended, and what was discussed at these briefings?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Mostly when there was no combat going on, every day at a certain time there would be a briefing. During combat, we would mostly meet at the forward command post of the OZ, where the commander of the OZ would attend, and his assistants, and the commanders of the units located in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: And what would you discuss at these briefings?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Well, mostly we would discuss how many men we had, the positions we had reached, whether there had been any fighting, whether we suffered any losses. We would discuss matters of logistics and any problems that might have arisen, and we would be given assignments for the forthcoming period, that is to say, for the following day.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Andabak, now let's move on. We're going to skip two documents and move on to document P -- 5D04385. It is an order from Colonel Siljeg, dated June 1993, and linked to reporting of the commands, the regular combat reports. Now, did you receive this order?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, we did receive this order and acted upon it. And as it says in the order, we executed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Right. We'll skip the next document and move on to document 5D02102. And while we're waiting for that document to be displayed, let me ask you this, Mr. Andabak: In your OZ, who issued you orders for combat in your OZ?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: The commander of the operative zone, himself, issued orders to me, personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Andabak, were you ever involved in some combat outside the North-West Herzegovina OZ?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, we were involved in the South-East Herzegovina OZ.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what the principle was, how you went from your zone to the South-East Herzegovina OZ? Who gave you the orders to go? How does this function, generally speaking? What's the procedure?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Well, the command of the South-East Herzegovina Operative Zone asking for assistance in manpower, that is to say, the military police, sends a request to the Main Staff of the HVO, and the Main Staff issues this same order to the Military Police Administration. And then the head of the Military Police Administration issues the order for this unit to move from one zone to another.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: And when you arrive in that area of responsibility, once you arrive, who issues you orders in that new area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: The commander does, the commander of the operative zone in which we are located, or the person that he authorises to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Now look at the document that you have before you, 5D02102. It's an order from Colonel Zeljko Siljeg, dated the 29th of June, 1993, and it says: "The military police forces in Bugojno and Gornji Vakuf are placed under the command of the Eugen Kvaternik and Ante Starcevic Brigades in their area of responsibility. "In addition to their regular tasks, the military police forces are also combat units and should be used -- and can be used as such." Tell me, Mr. Andabak, did you receive this order?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: As commander of the battalion, yes, I did receive this order.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: And was the order carried out?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, the order was carried out, and these two military police companies were placed under the command specified.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Now, in item 3, it says: "This order is valid until it is changed by the Administration of the Military Police or the Command of the OZ." Now, was this order, in fact, changed, amended at all?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, the order was changed pursuant to an order from the commander of the OZ.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Once again, we're going to skip the next document and move on to document P05478. This is an order from Mr. Coric, dated the 29th of September, 1993, and this is what the order says: "Pursuant to an order from the main command of the HVO -- Main Staff of the HVO, I hereby issue the following order: "Urgently send the 3rd Company of the 2nd Light Assault Battalion of the Military Police to the Gornji Vakuf Sector. The company commander is to report to the forward command post at Prozor, to the commander of the Operative Zone of North-West Herzegovina." Mr. Andabak, tell us, please, why does Mr. Coric -- why is Mr. Coric writing this order, when you've told us that the 2nd Light Assault Battalion was within the composition of the OZ of North-West Herzegovina? Can you explain that to me, please?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: The 3rd Company of the 2nd Light Assault Battalion of the Military Police was engaged in carrying out its orders and assignments on the Mostar front; that is to say, in the OZ of South-East Herzegovina. As I explained a moment ago, the commander of the North-West Herzegovina Operative Zone asked for the withdrawal of this unit from Mostar, and he asked that it be activated in the operative zone under his command. And in keeping with that, the Main Staff then issued an order to the military police to relocate, and the chief of the military police, Valentin Coric, issued this order to the 3rd Company's 2nd Light Assault Battalion, ordering it to go and carry out assignments in the North-West Herzegovina Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to my colleague. But with respect to the answer we've just heard a moment ago, and that was on page 36, lines 11 to 16, there was obviously a mistake in the transcript, because the same matter is being talked about, but it was stated differently. So perhaps you should return to your question and ask the witness again. There's something missing from the transcript, but I didn't want to intervene. But in view of the answer the witness has just given us, now, I don't want to speak because I may be accused of leading the witness. Anyway, it was the witness's answer on page 36, beginning with line 11. Perhaps the best thing would be if you were to ask your question again, Counsel, because what the witness said a moment ago is different to what he said then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Witness, just briefly, to clarify matters, a very short question: Who requests reinforcement for the military police force?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: The command of the operative zone from the Main Staff, if the military police is from another operative zone. So the Main Staff issues an order to the Military Police Administration, and the Military Police Administration acts upon it.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: All right, fine. We can skip the next document, and let's go to P03778. This is a document dated the 28th of July, 1993, in which Mr. Coric says that pursuant to an order from the head of the Defence Department, he orders as follows; and enumerates the light assault battalions, and says that in operational terms for military operations, they are to be re-subordinated to the commander of the HVO or the commander of the corresponding zone specifically authorised by the commander. Can you explain what that means? What is this about, and is there any difference here if we were to compare it to what we were discussing earlier on?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, there is a difference, because by this order all the units are being re-subordinated to the commander of the HVO, who can deploy the units mentioned in any area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: All right, fine, Mr. Andabak. Tell me now, in the penultimate paragraph of that same order, it says that the assistant chiefs are duty-bound -- in addition to deploying these military police units in battle and their re-subordination to the commander of the HVO, they are also duty-bound to secure permanent links, functional links, between all the military police units and their links towards the Military Police Administration. Now, you were assistant chief for a time, so tell us what that means. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: That means that the military police, not engaged in battle and which has free days or is on furlough, can continue their military police -- regular military police work, performing military police assignments. So everything with respect to reporting, sending reports, and so on, that that should be continued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. If I may just ask a question on document P03778. The police light assault brigades are re-subordinated to the commander of the HVO. Could you give us the name of that commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the commander of the HVO at that point in time was Mr. Slobodan Praljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. The other possibility would have been Mr. Boban, but your answer clarifies. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, it didn't escape me that this document is dated 28th of July. We know that General Praljak took up his post a few days before that. This document shows that General Praljak would like to have under his direct authority the various battalions, because according to this document, those battalions will be re-subordinated to the commander of the HVO. So, in a way, it's the Chief of Staff; hence the question from my colleague, because there could be some confusion and we could have thought it could have been Mr. Mate Boban. But you gave us a very clear answer in this regard. So according to you, what meaning should we pay to this document, because it is some sort of a small revolution, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I wouldn't put it that way, and I don't know what I can actually tell you about that. Anyway, all these units mentioned here, because of the deployment of the units on the ground and so that they could go into action as quickly as possible, I would say it was to bypass the red tape, because having one commander writing to another commander and so on, all that red tape takes a lot of time, so to cut that short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: During this period after this order, who was in operative command of the assistant commanders in the field?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: It was still the commander of the OZ.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's skip one document, and let's go to P040251 -- P04251. This is an order issued by Mr. Petkovic in August 1993. It was sent to all operative zones. It deals with the freedom of movement of UN forces. Did you receive this order?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: I received the order via the command of the operative zone.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Did you act upon it?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Of course. We were duty-bound to carry that order out.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Let's move on to the following document, after having skipped one. This is P04063. This is another order issued by Mr. Petkovic in August 1993, dealing with bringing back deserters. Did you receive this order?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: We received this order also through the command of the OZ.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Did you carry it out?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: The 6th Active Service Battalion brought back soldiers in its operative zone, and it sent daily reports to the commander of the OZ about the number of soldiers who were brought who either didn't respond to the mobilisation calls or were absent without leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, we are going to skip a few documents. Unfortunately, I have to skip documents because I don't have enough time. And let's go to 5D03104. Please tell me when you find it.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: This is a permit signed by you in October 1993. Is this a permit that you issued? Could you please tell me something about the document? What do you know about it?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: This is a permit for passage through all military police check-points in the zone. It is based on the order of the Main Staff, after a verbal consent of the OZ commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Were you authorised to issue such permits on your own, independently?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. I couldn't do it on my own. I couldn't do any -- I couldn't issue any permits independently.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Let's go to the following document, which is P01238. This is an order issued in January 1993, co-signed by the Chief of the Main Staff of the HVO, Mr. Milivoj Petkovic, and on behalf of the BH Army Staff, Commander Arif Pasalic. Let's look at bullet point 4 in this order, which refers to the blockade and lifting the blockade off the roads. Did you receive this order?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: I received this order in the Prozor IKM, where the command of the OZ was located. The military police acted upon the agreement and the order issued by the two chiefs, i.e., the Chief of the Main Staff and Mr. Pasalic on behalf of the BH Army Staff, and we reported back to the commander of the OZ about what we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Let's now skip a couple of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You might be able to answer this question. Here we see, under 4 of this document, the question of humanitarian convoys. Did you personally control the humanitarian convoy? Did you do that personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As the assistant commander of the MP Administration, I participated in the establishment of joint check-points in the zone. And when it comes to the control of the humanitarian transport, it was done by the military police which was on the spot, and the military police did their job without any problems. And as far as acting as escorts and things like that, nobody ever asked for such services from us when it came to humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I wanted to know is this: whether you, yourself, personally controlled a humanitarian convoy one day. I'm not talking about the documents. I'm talking about you physically controlling a humanitarian convoy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, we are going to skip three documents, and let's go to P02836. The document was issued by the 3rd Battalion of the Herceg Stjepan Brigade from Jablanica. Jablanica was part of the North-West Herzegovina OZ, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, it was under the Herceg Stjepan Brigade from Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: This was signed by the battalion commander, who issues an order to the military police in Jablanica to set up a check-point. Under 3, he provides for patrols, and under 4 he says: "This order enters into force immediately. Commander Azinovic is responsible ..." Did you know about this order? Was it ever implemented, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: I was aware of this order. It was implemented when an order came -- or when a request came from the Herceg Stjepan Brigade from Konjic arrived in the operative zone. And when such request was received, this order was carried out, and the OZ commander and the brigade commander were informed thereof.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: By way of introduction into the following topic, Mr. Andabak, tell me, what is the meaning of the area of responsibility of the commander, and how is it determined?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: The area of responsibility of a commander is the front-line; for example, from one elevation to another, from one trig point to another, and it is determined by width and in depth. That zone of responsibility can be 300 to 500 metres in depth, not more. But if there is a village behind the front-line, whether abandoned or a village with mixed Bosniak Croatian or Serb Muslim population, the commander will put his troops behind the village in order to have the control of the entire village. And he made this decision with his assistant for security. He had his brigade police which secured his command wherever he put it. And that same brigade military police controlled the entry and exits -- entry to and exits from the zone of responsibility and performed policing duties within the zone of responsibility should some events of that nature occur. And the zone of responsibility in depth could be anything up to 10 or even 15 kilometres. But I also know, for example, that the entire city of Mostar was the zone of responsibility for a commander under the command of the commander of the operative zone, and it was divided into various sectors.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Andabak. And now tell me, what are the responsibilities of a commander in his area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: First of all, he is to look after the security of that zone. He has to make sure that no crimes are committed, that there's no breaches of discipline, thefts. He has to protect the population that resides in his area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Andabak, what are the duties of a commander if a crime takes place in his area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: If he received the information about a crime that happened, together with his brigade police, he will go to the crime scene. He will secure the crime scene. He will preserve any clues and traces, if such clues and traces existed. If they found the perpetrator on the spot, he will keep them, and he can keep them -- keep him on the premises until the arrival of the military police.
