And if a crime was committed, he can, himself, file a criminal report, or it can be done by his assistant for security, but he can file the criminal report himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: If I understand you properly, he can do it on his own, or he can inform the military police and ask them to do that. If I understand you properly, there are two possibilities in that case.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes. If a crime requires the presence of the Criminal Department of the Military Police, they will come to the scene and do everything necessary to file a criminal report.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Andabak, let's look at the following document after skipping one, P04819. This is an order issued by the commander of the Main Staff, Mr. Slobodan Praljak, P04819. The order was issued in September 1993 and refers to the regulation of the area of responsibility and combat activities, and he says here: "I order:" Under 1: "The area of responsibility ..." And he determines the left border of the area of responsibility, and he says: " ... in front of the current defence line in depth towards the municipalities of Livno which are not under the occupation of the enemy forces." Tell me, how is the area of responsibility determined in Livno municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Actually, the Serbian artillery could open mortar fire on Livno, so Livno, in one part, was a part of the area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: What you know from the field about the area of responsibility, does this reflect the bullet point 1 in this document?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: I wouldn't know, because I don't know what is the previous order that General Praljak refers to. But this order obviously removes some ambiguities that the commanders might have had at that time, and the order was issued.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: And now let's skip -- let's skip two documents, and let's look at the third document, which is P03135. This is an order issued by the Knez Domagoj Brigade commander, dated 3rd of July, 1993, and he says in this order, based on the newly-arisen situation in the zone of responsibility of the 1st Brigade, and due to increased crime and unwanted behaviour by some commanders and soldiers, and pursuant to the extension of the area of responsibility, "I hereby," under number 1: "Prevent any theft or any other form of appropriation of personal and other property of people, arrest the perpetrators and institute criminal proceedings again them through this command." Under number 3 it says: "Prevent any violent behaviour, arrest perpetrators and start proceedings against them though this command." Under 4, it says: "Offer protection to the civilian population." And then under 11, it says: "The commanders of units, in person, shall be responsible for the implementation of this order." Mr. Andabak, I know that this does not originate from your area of responsibility, but I would welcome your brief comment and tell me what the situation was in your area of responsibility. Did the brigade commanders act in the same way as the commander whose order we have just looked at?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Every order -- or, rather, not all orders could be the same. This brigade commander looked at the situation. He received information from the field, and he ordered for the shortcomings of which he was informed or noticed himself to be removed. And every commander could either add or subtract or alter things as needed in order to warn other soldiers not to commit crimes, thefts, to refrain from disorderly behaviour, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the following document, which is P00 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Document 003135 concerns the area of responsibility of Colonel Obradovic. You are, therefore, not concerned by this document. Nonetheless, I would like to have your view on this item 7. If you look at item 7, this has to do with the Muslim population, where it is being asked that they be re-grouped in that area and secured upon your orders. How do you interpret this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, most probably in that zone houses were scattered. I don't know how this is going to be interpreted, the word "scattered." And in order to prevent crimes against the population in the area, I suppose that they re-grouped them in an area where the houses were closer to each other, and that was all done in order to secure those people and for him to be sure that those people were secure. For example, you have one house on one hilltop, another on another hilltop, and the third one between the two. I don't know if you understood my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, I'm sure you realise that this was the 3rd of July; i.e., a few days after the 30th of June. In your area of responsibility, your own area of responsibility, was this kind of order given, or were you in charge of the Muslims and made sure that they were protected properly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, I can't tell you that. I don't know whether the situation was the same in other zones of responsibility. I know that I did not have my own zone of responsibility. We were always subordinated to either the brigade or the unit that was in that area of responsibility, and so I wouldn't know, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me fine-tune my question. Were you aware of the fact, at your level, that military policemen, upon the orders of brigade commanders of the area of responsibility in the north-west - I'm being very specific - were assigned after the 30th of June, 1993, to re-group Muslim civilians or to disarm HVO soldiers who were Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, I'm not aware of that. I don't know. All I can say is -- and tell you what happened in Livno or in Tomislavgrad, when, under the brigade command, the Bosniak population were disarmed; members of the BH Army within the composition of the HVO, those people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you disarmed them in Livno. After they had been disarmed, did you regroup them, isolate them, detain them, monitored, guarded, thrown in jail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, following an order from the brigade commander, we isolated those people and put them in two school buildings - and I think there was a third building used too - until the conflict passed. They were under protection and, on the second or third day, were allowed to go home. They were released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, you are saying that they were guarded for two to three days. Then they were released, and they left freely. Where did they go when they could leave freely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, they went back home to their families, their houses and their families.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Andabak, to follow on from that, you said you received an order to disarm, if I understood you correctly -- the Muslims, to disarm the Muslims who were HVO members; is that right? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Now, in your military police battalion, did you have any Muslim members?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, I did, I had some Muslims in my battalion, and the commander of the 2nd Light Assault Battalion, Jasarevic, was a Muslim himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Did you disarm them?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: No, we didn't disarm Muslim members of the military police. We checked some of them out and saw that they were not a threat to security anyway, so those people remained in our ranks until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Now would you look at the next document, which is P00778.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Colonel, you've just said something which I believe is important. You mentioned it very quickly. I discover, because this is something I did not know, that in the 2nd Battalion of the Military Police there were Muslims, you examined the situation, you did not disarm them, and you said very briefly that they remained until the end of the war in your units. So how many were they, these Muslims that remained in the military police of the HVO, in percentage terms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For my battalion, Your Honour, I can tell you that they were between 25 and 30 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ranging between 25 and 30 per cent. I don't know what the figure is, because [as interpreted] I've seen a document to that effect. How many men did you have in the 2nd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the 2nd Battalion, Your Honour, depending on the period of time, but between 540 to 580 men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, ranging from 25 to 30 per cent, that would mean that there were at least 100 Muslims in the military police of the 2nd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, thereabouts, if you take all the companies, including the commands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, look at P00778, the next document now, please. We've skipped a few. This is a document from the brigade commander, the Ante Starcevic Brigade from Vakuf, dated November 1992, in which he says that on the 17th of November, 1992, a member of "our unit" committed a gruesome murder and killed citizen Salih Grizic. And lower down, it says that: "The criminal Ratko Rajic, in the spirit of the provisions of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, we escorted him to the Military Prosecutor's Office in Mostar." Now, do you know about this event, Mr. Andabak?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, I do, I know about this event, and the brigade commander acted very properly, as he should have done. This is a very important document, and Mr. Tokic is writing to the Municipal Staff of the Territorial Defence of Gornji Vakuf, apologising for the incident, and that he would like good neighbourly relations to be restored in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Now look at the next document, P01359, dated the 30th of January, 1993, which Mr. Siljeg is sending to all the brigades, and writes it on the basis of an order from the Chief of the Main Staff. He says here, in item 1, that the soldiers, non-commissioned officers, and officers must do their best to prevent all acts not in keeping with International War Law. And then in item 13, it says that the SIS and the military police will arrest any pilferers, keep them in detention, record all the items looted and stolen; and, in item 16, says that these commanders should their own orders down the line. Tell me, did you receive this order?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, we received this order from the command of the operative zone in which we were active, and our task was to establish check-points on the territory, and anybody engaging in criminal activities, smuggling and anything else, should be detained if they threaten security in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Did you act upon it, did you do that?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes. A member of the military police in the OZ was informed, all the people were informed, and we informed the command of the OZ about the measures we had taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Look at the next document now, please. P02832 is the number. It is the minutes from an on-site investigation compiled by the Ante Starcevic Brigade's military police. It is an on-site investigation conducted in the village of Bistrica after Ramiz Basevic was killed. Now, do you know about this occurrence? Did you hear about this happening?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear about this, and the military police -- the brigade military police acted according to orders received from the brigade commander; that is to say, that every incident in the area of responsibility, and this was one such instance, that this military policeman, Jakovljevic, compiled the minutes, and the matter was processed further and the investigations into the perpetrator conducted.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Andabak, you, as a military policeman, did you undergo any training at all teaching you about International Humanitarian Law, International War Law, and things like that?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: I graduated from Police School, and during my training and education there, one of the subjects taught was International Humanitarian Law. I know that the personnel from the 2nd Military Police Battalion were also educated in that subject when they underwent training and education at the Training Centre in Neum. And I, myself, organised education courses on that subject in the battalion command and in individual companies, organised with the help of the International Red Cross, where we received booklets about the conduct of soldiers in combat.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, I'm going to skip over a few documents, and I'm going to try and bring my examination to a close.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While listening to you, I was looking at the document P2832. We see that a crime was committed at 2330 hours on the 17th of June, 1993. According to the details, it seems that a vehicle, a Golf Audi, was seen close to his house with two men on board. We know that when war is raging, and there is always an increase in criminal activity. So I was wondering whether, within the military police, you had night patrols that had been ordered in order to check on everyone that would be moving around, and was there not a curfew that would have been ordered? Because those individuals that were moving around or that were on board this vehicle, and they seem to be the perpetrator of this crime, they were on this road, which means that there was no checks on the roads at night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this was the Gornji Vakuf area, so there wasn't a curfew in force there. And since this was in the area of responsibility, then police check-points were set up. The village of Bistrica is along the main road, so you could just cross the road and you would be in another village, Trnovaca. Now, I don't know whether the military police had a check-point at the entrance and exit to the village, but judging by this, they didn't. And we didn't enter into the area of responsibility. That's up to the unit commander, who could form night patrols. Now, whether he did do that, I really can't say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, we're going to skip a few documents, and if we have time, we'll come back to them. But let's deal with document 5D02077. And while you're looking for that document, which is six documents on, tell me, Mr. Andabak, whether you know what the position was of the Military Police Administration towards members of the military police who acted in an undisciplined way and who perhaps committed crimes. Do you know about that, what their position was on crime?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, I do know about that, and it was the position of the military police, from the top man, Mr. Coric, was that any such perpetrators should be persecuted and a criminal report filed, and for them to be dismissed from the unit. And those who upset law and order, that disciplinary measures be taken against them and, if need be, to eliminate them from our units. So at all briefings and all my contacts with the Military Police Administration, also told us that anybody who besmirched the name of the military police on battlegrounds throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina, that they should be thrown out of the units.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Andabak, does the name Ilija Franjic ring a bell? Do you know the man? Is it familiar?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, I do know Ilija Franjic. I met him in 1992, when he was the commander of the Rama Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Have you found the document I mentioned? If so, look at it. It's dated the 6th of December, 1992. The document is signed by Ilija Franjic, as the commander of the Rama Brigade. Now, to the best of your knowledge, was he, indeed, the commander of that brigade at that period?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: From this document, we can see that he was commander of the Rama Brigade and that he wanted to leave the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Andabak, Mr. Ilija Franjic, what post did he occupy in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Well, I think it was in February 1993 that the municipal authorities recommended him as a commander of a police company, the military police company in Rama.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Now, when he was in the Rama Brigade, was he part of your battalion, which means that you were his senior officer?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, the military police company from Prozor did come within the composition of the 2nd Military Police Battalion. And as I was the commander of the Military Police Battalion, then, yes, that would be right.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Franjic report to you?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Mr. Franjic was obliged to report -- that his company should, on a daily basis, send reports to the officer on duty in the battalion, and he carried out all his tasks during the time that he was company commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Andabak, in his reports, did he ever warn you and say that the military police was engaged in some criminal acts and crime in the Prozor area, generally?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: No, he never wrote anything like that, nor did he warn me or provide me with any other information whereby military policemen engaged in unlawful activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Now look at 5D02139, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, I would thank your counsel to have asked the question, but if she hadn't asked this question, I would have asked it myself. Over the last few months or perhaps years, we have received documents that are rather alarming regarding the behaviour of military policemen based in Prozor. There were reports from the SIS, amongst others, and it was saying that there was officers from the military police were committing various crimes, from theft, but other types of crimes as well, and we had the feeling that all this was deriving from the fact that no one was able to stop them and to punish them, and in a way it was, more or less, chaos. So your counsel has asked this question, and you said you were not aware. Under oath, you are hereby saying that you never heard of this sort of behaviour happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we knew that crimes were committed, but we didn't know that they were committed by military police. The SIS could write whatever they wanted to, but they never accused us. I never received a document warning me that they were committing crime that would have required me to act. I did act finally when I learned at one of the brief that is Mr. Franjic had caused problems about some passes, and then, as the commander of the military police, I informed the MP Administration about that, as soon as I received the information, and then I issued an order to him to write a written report about his actions and behaviour. He did, but he never reported back to me, but to the Administration of the Military Police, when he left the military police. As soon as I learned, I asked him to write a report about his behaviour, but immediately when I did that, he resigned from the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, do you have the document before you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. I may be a bit retarded this afternoon, but I am not quite clear. Mr. Andabak, what is it that Mr. Franjic cries out, I am not -- I am no longer able to carry out this duty? What does he mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know. If you are talking about the order that I have before me now, or, rather, this document before me, either he was in a mental state or he was not a stable commander. I really can't tell you, I'm not in a position to tell you. Something was wrong with him, personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, we'll hear what the relevance of this document is to be, then. But I find it a bit difficult to give it some meaning if that is the case. Would you agree that this is not a very clear document, that it's not easy to draw any conclusions from it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, after he said that he was no longer capable, that was that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let's make one thing clear. My only objective was to establish that at that moment the gentleman was the brigade commander, and that's the only reason why I showed the document, and that's what I asked the witness. I just wanted to demonstrate who he was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Do you have 5D02139 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: This is a report issued by Mr. Ilija Franjic, as the commander of the Military Police Company. It was sent to the HVO in Rama municipality. Did you know that Mr. Franjic reported to the Rama municipality HVO, to the municipal authorities there?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: I see this report now and didn't know that he reported about the work of the military police in Rama. There was no need for him to report to the municipality of Rama, being a member of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Let me take you back to something that you said previously in answer to the Presiding Judge's question. You said, As soon as I learned that Ilija Franjic did dishonourable things. When was it that you first learned about that?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: I learned about his dishonourable act at a briefing in the OZ sometime in autumn 1993. I learned that he was being bossy, that he was bossing people.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Okay, you said that. I'd like to know what you did when you learnt about that. Let's take things step by step. What was your first reaction?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: After the briefing, I called the MP Administration. I don't know whether I told them -- I told the chief of the MP Administration or his deputy, and then I went to Franjic's office and ordered him to write a short report about the relevant events and his behaviour about which I'd heard earlier that evening at the briefing.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at 5D02049. This is a report by Franjic, sent to the Military Police Administration, a report about his work before the 21st of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm still with the previous document. Could I be told why -- or what indicates that this document, which has "Military Police - Rama" as a sender, and then is illegibly, it appears, signed by the VP unit commander? Are we sure this is still Mr. Franjic, the person who half a year earlier had resigned with immediate effect, Mr. Andabak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, we didn't know why he resigned from the brigade. But I repeat, he was appointed as the commander of the MP company by the municipal authorities, and perhaps Mr. Franjic felt that he should report to the municipality about his work.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, maybe I can help. The resignation that was issued six months before that was a resignation from the brigade, and after that he became an MP. The document, when he says, I've had it, I can no longer remain in the position, the position in question is the position of the brigade commander. That's what he resigned from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, and we just take the witness's word for it that what he told us about his later being nominated as chief of the military police of the brigade is, in fact, factual?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Whether it's true, we'll have to finally -- we'll have to say, but I have understood correctly what has gone on. Thank you, and excuse me for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, if I understood you properly, he was the commander of the Military Police Company in Prozor from the month of February 1993; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Now, in front of us we have that report entitled "A Report About My Work as Commander of the Rama-Prozor Military Police" during the period between the 10th of February, 1993, and the 21st September 1993. At the end of the document, before the signature, Mr. Franjic says: "I hereby submit my irrevocable resignation." Mr. Andabak, in answering the Trial Chamber's questions, you said that after you held him to task about what you'd heard at the briefing, that he submitted a report and that he submitted his resignation at the same time. Is this the report, the one that you have before you at the moment?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's the report. He ignored me, as the battalion commander at the moment, and he approached directly the Military Police Administration, and he talked to them directly. He bypassed me.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, do you know what happened next with Mr. Franjic? What transpired?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: As far as I know, Mr. Franjic, after submitting a resignation to the military police, he returned to the Rama Brigade Command as the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: And did anything happen in respect of the crimes of which you'd heard at the briefing?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: We sent crime police to Prozor-Rama. They took stock of all the unsolved crimes. We reinforced the military police, and we brought military police officers from other OZs, and we carried out an arrest of Mr. Ilija Franjic and "his men," in inverted commas. They were not his men, but men who were with him. They were questioned, they were subject to investigation, and I don't know what happened with that case after that. That was in late November 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, could you please look at 3D00422. The date is 20 January 1994. This is an official note made by the military police, which says: "Due to the rape of Muslim women, the following persons or individuals have to be brought in:" Two names are listed under 1 and 2, and then there is a list of six people thereafter. Mr. Andabak, you said that Franjic had been arrested in November, and what is happening here? Who is being arrested pursuant to this document? Who had been arrested, who was being arrested, at the time this document was issued?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: According to this document, Zoran Calis and Jure Petrovic had to be arrested for the crime of rape, and the rest of the information was provided to the Crime Prevention Service which had not completed the investigation by then, and the information would be of some use in further investigation and proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: And as for the remaining six, had they already been arrested before that?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: I really can't remember their names, but most of them had been arrested already.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, we're moving to a new topic just briefly. Were you in any way involved in the conflicts which took place in Prozor towards the end of October 1993? If that was the case, can you tell us something about that? I apologise. In 1992. I misspoke, I gave you the wrong year. It's 1992.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, I was involved in the armed conflicts there, and the reason was that I found myself spontaneously in the Prozor municipality, and my primary task was to take a military police company, composed of locals of Tomislavgrad, Livno and Posusje, and head across Travnik and engage in combat in order to help the citizens of Jajce, which was encircled by the Serbs at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: So how did you find yourself there? Who -- okay, let's take things from the head. Who issued the order for you to go to Jajce?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: A verbal order was given to us by the deputy chief of the MP Administration, Mr. Lavric, and he told us to go to Vitez first to report to the commander of the OZ, Mr. Blaskic. But when we arrived in Prozor in the early-morning hours, the commander of the military police in Prozor informed me that he had received instructions from the MP Administration to go to Travnik, because Mr. Blaskic was already there and from there he would transport us to Jajce. In the early-morning hours, we arrived at the Karamustafic check-point at the entrance to Gornji Vakuf --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. The document 3D0522 [as interpreted] is actually under seal, so it should not be broadcast outside this courtroom. I will give the number again, 3D00422.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the Trial Chamber. I missed that completely. I did not realise that it was under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Let's see where we left it off. You said that you arrived at the Karamustafic check-point?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, that was in the early-morning hours, about half past 4.00 or 5.00. We were met at barricades on the road. Those were barricades made of tree trunks. On the left-hand side from the check-point, there was a machine-gun nests manned by the Mujahedin, and I can say that for a fact because they sported beards and they were different from our men. And at the check-point, itself, a military policeman from the ABiH approached me, and when I asked him what was going on, he said that I should go back to where I came from, that I could not go through.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at P00670. The document was issued by Mr. Praljak and Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Just a moment. Bear with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: You have to go back a bit.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: It says here -- I can't see the number, but it says: "At this time, we're trying to move an HVO armed formation in the direction of Jajce, and their strength is about 400 armed men." Mr. Andabak, do you know what armed formation is in question here?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Well, it's the armed formation of the military police, numbering 100 to 120 men, and there was also a unit that had passed through before me, which was a mixed Croatian/Bosniak unit going to Jajce, commanded by Ante Prkoca [phoen], and they were going to Jajce's reinforcement.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, you told us earlier on that you did not submit combat reports to the Military Police Administration. Now I'd like to ask you to look at the document P00712. You said that you included -- you became involved in the combat in Prozor spontaneously, but it says here -- well, this is a report which you are sending to Mr. Coric, and it is titled "Report on the Events in the Prozor Municipality and Gornji Vakuf Municipality." Now, why did you submit this report to Mr. Coric in the first place?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: As commander, I did not arrive at the spot where I was ordered to go, and I wanted to inform the chief of the military police with the activities that the military police had engaged in during that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Andabak. Now tell me this: Were you involved in the events -- or, rather, conflicts in Gornji Vakuf at the beginning of January 1993, you or your unit? Was it involved in any of that?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, I was involved, and so was my unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Would you look at P01053 next, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second, Colonel. The question regarding Prozor is important, because it is in the indictment. According to the Prosecutor's case, in October, and more precisely on the 25th of October, 1992, the HVO launched an operation in order to arrest Muslims and to force them to leave the town. I will not go into further details. This is the case of the Prosecution. You said that you were there in Prozor, so what is interesting is to hear your version. Do you agree with the case of the Prosecution, namely, that it's the HVO that launched the attack, or do you disagree? And if you disagree, why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't agree with what it says in the indictment, as far as the allegations and accusations about Prozor are concerned, because I know full well that the Croatian forces, whether military or municipal, together with the Bosniak side, as far as I know, and I heard about this, talked about easing tensions in Gornji Vakuf. So I'm telling you about what I heard. And I know that the conflict broke out, and the brigade commander, of the Rama Brigade, that is, that the Bosniaks had killed a Croat and seriously wounded another, and that this other Croat, after he passed away -- well, that's how the conflict started between the Croats and Bosniaks in Prozor, with the killing of two citizens or, rather, two Croatian soldiers, although efforts were being made to calm tensions on both sides. And my soldiers, when they returned from that check-point, well, 90 per cent of them were to be found in the Bosniak cafes. They socialised with the Bosniaks. One of them worked in the hydroelectric power company of Jablanica. And they socialised and were deciding when to meet next, but the conflict broke out that very evening. But there was no organised attack against the Bosniaks to disarm them or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as you know, what did the HOS do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can't commend the HOS in that operation at all -- in that conflict, I meant to say - not "operation," "conflict" - because I was almost killed by them, myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Give us some details.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, mostly, whether they were HOS men or whatever, but I saw that insignia, Your Honour, on the sleeves of these men, and I know that -- well, in my opinion - I'm giving you my own opinion - that their prime task was looting, and I heard people say, while some people were engaged in combat, they would be looting, taking cameras, bottles of whiskey, or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, well, I asked you whether you were involved in the Gornji Vakuf events of January 1993, and for that I asked you to look at P01053, which is a report from Mr. Coric in which he states that you were given the assignment of carrying out the relocation of police units of the 2nd Battalion and 1st Active Military Police Battalion, and he says that the main task of this assignment was to preserve law and order, the protection of the population and inhabited areas, to restore road traffic, and defuse fear among the Croatian population in the said municipalities. Now, Mr. Andabak, tell me this: Did you receive this assignment with these contents? Do you remember having received that?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember receiving this document, setting out my main assignments.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived -- or, rather, let's look at the next document first. So we're skipping one document and going on to P01350, and that will be the last document that we're going to discuss. It's the minutes from the meeting held on the 27th of January, 1993, on the premises of the Military Police Centre in Ljubuski. Tell me now, Mr. Andabak, did you attend that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, I did attend the meeting with my subordinate commanders.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Do you know who convened the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: As far as I know, the meeting was convened by General Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: And what was discussed at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Well, mostly the situation in Gornji Vakuf and Central Bosnia was discussed, and logistics support to the military police, replenishment of personnel, the role of the military police in general, its training and education. And we learnt some lessons, what could be done, what couldn't be done. And that was the first time that we saw Mr. Coric. He issued an order to us in the previous document, and he was in Zagreb at the time, so he didn't know that we were involved in the Gornji Vakuf operations and combat. So this was an opportunity for him to talk to us and to hear about our activities in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: And who was your commander while you were in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: In Gornji Vakuf, we were under the command of the operative zone. And when we were in the town of Vakuf, itself, we were under the command of the Ante Starcevic Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Tell us, at this meeting did anybody mention the fact that members of the military police, during these events in Gornji Vakuf had committed any unlawful acts, such as setting fire to houses, looting property, and the like?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: No, that was not discussed, nobody mentioned anything like that, and there was information that that did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. That concludes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Tomasegovic Tomic, for having abided by the two hours that had been allocated to you. We shall have a break now and resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session, so we're going to start with Mr. Stojic's Defence. And, Ms. Nozica, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I would like to greet everybody in the courtroom, and I would like to inform the Trial Chamber that I have 32 minutes for my cross-examination, pursuant to your decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Andabak. I can see that you have been provided with my set of documents, and I believe that everybody else has received them as well. Mr. Andabak, earlier today, on page 35 of today's transcript, on line 12, you spoke about meetings or briefings in the OZ, and you said that you attended those briefings at the -- in the office of the commander of the OZ. Could you tell the Trial Chamber whether the assistant commander of the OZ for SIS, IPD, and Medical Services, was also present at those briefings?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Madam Counsel, the persons you mentioned attended each briefing or were replaced by persons appointed by them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, you said that you received orders from the OZ commander; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Were the orders both oral and written, or either/or written?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Both orders, both oral and written.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And I'm trying to focus on the assistants for SIS, IPD, and Medical Services. At those briefings that you attended, did those persons inform the OZ commander about having performed tasks and orders that they had previously received from the commander?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Madam, as far as I can remember, the officers for IPD and Medical Services did, but I believe that the assistant for security did not brief the OZ commander before us because of the nature of his duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, are you saying that the assistant for SIS reported directly to the commander of the OZ about the performance of the tasks that he had received?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: I would say so, most probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you now look at P970. I've not prepared it because it was shown to you a while ago. Your going to see it in e-court. This is a report. We're going to see it very shortly on e-court. Yes, that's it. This is a report that you've already spoken about and answered questions put to you by Mr. Coric's counsel, and you said that the handwritten addition, "SIS," is the handwriting of Mr. Siljeg, who was the commander of the OZ; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber whether you can recognise the family name that you see beneath the word "SIS"?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: This is the assistant commander of our OZ for SIS, Mr. Drago Banovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, does this list mean that Mr. Siljeg forwarded your report to his assistant for SIS, Mr. Drago Banovic?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Precisely, and this document is signed over to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, with regard to document P4110, describing the situation in Mokronoge, you spoke about that on page 32, lines 13 through 18, and His Honour Judge Antonetti asked you why the brigade military police called SIS. Was that the brigade SIS which was under the same command as the brigade military police?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, it was the SIS of the Krajl Tomislav Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Andabak. And now I would like us to try and clarify an ambiguity that His Honour Judge Trechsel pointed to. Could the Court please produce P1099, 1099. This is the brigade's schematic which we've already seen. Please wait for a moment and you will see it. His Honour Judge Trechsel pointed to the following fact -- could we please move on to the following page, both in Croatian and in English, please. Yes, that's it. We can collate the original with the translator, and we can see that some information under column 10, 14 and 15 were added subsequently by hand. Isn't that so, Mr. Andabak?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, the names of the commanders and people in the staff were added by hand under columns 10, 14 and 15.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: His Honour Judge Trechsel asked you whether it was possible for the commander to have 380 vehicles at his disposal. But if we look further down, we can see that his deputy, if the figure were to be correct, also had 370, then the co-ordinator for social welfare had 350 vehicles. I will not ask you to make any speculations, but I'm sure that you can't explain the figures; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yeah, that's right. I really don't know where the figures came from and what they mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And now could you please look at the first document in the binder, which is 2D01370. For the transcript, I'm going to say that document 2D01370 is another schematic of the brigade establishment without any handwritten additions, so it is in its original form. And I would also like to say that the document has already been admitted into evidence. Look at it for yourself, the second page of the document, or maybe you can go through all the pages, and you will be able to see very clearly that this is actually the original schematic without any handwritten additions or added information. I'm waiting for your answer, sir.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, this is the original schematic without the names or anything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Andabak, could we please look at the following document, which is P610. That's the next document in my binder. This is a daily report by Mr. Valentin Coric, and I am going to ask you only about the first paragraph in this daily report, where it says because of the events in Central Bosnia, pursuant to the: "On the order of the head of the Defence Department, we sent a reinforcement from the 2nd Battalion ..." Mr. Andabak, earlier today, on page 63, on lines from 2 to 3, you said that you had been sent to Jajce pursuant to an oral order issued by Mr. Rade Lavric; am I right? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: That's what I said, and, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: One could conclude, based on that, that you were not sent pursuant to an order by Mr. Stojic, actually that you never seen an order of that kind from Mr. Stojic; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I did not want to interrupt my learned friend. I wanted to make a correction on the transcript. On page 64, line 3, the name Rade Lavric was not recorded, although the witness did mention the gentleman's name. Am I right, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And now I would kindly ask you to look at the following document, which is P3146. This would be an order issued by Mr. Bruno Stojic on the 3rd of July, 1993, and that order was sent to the Petar Kresimir Brigade in Livno. In paragraph 1 of this order, it says that: "The Livno Military Police (company) under the command of Mr. Andabak, must be relocated to Mostar by 2000 hours on 3rd July 1993." Under 2, it says: "If the commander," or you, "fails to understand the newly-developed situation, criminal charges will be brought against him." And under 3: "The brigade command must deliver this order to Mr. Andabak," to you. Mr. Andabak, did you ever receive this order issued by Mr. Bruno Stojic?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Madam, I did not receive this order, but I heard about it at a later date.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, during that period of time did you arrive in Mostar? After the 30th of June, did you arrive in Mostar at all?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Madam, I didn't arrive in Mostar after I was sent there by the minister of defence, who told me to go there. I said on that occasion to the defence minister, Mr. Stojic, that I already had problems with the commander of the OZ, who accused me of deserting from the theatre of war and that I frequently went to Mostar in order to gain ranks or privileges, and our conversation stopped there. In the meantime, the Chief of the Main Staff, Mr. Petkovic, called me, and together with my unit, after that call I went to Mostar, and there I met with General Petkovic and with the defence minister in his office. I received my orders from General Petkovic because I knew that General Petkovic was the OZ commander's superior, and I was convinced that the two of them had an agreement about that order being issued to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, when did all that happen, on what day?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: It was on the 30th.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What month?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: It was on the 30th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When you arrived in Mostar with your unit, where were you deployed and by whom?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: When we arrived in Mostar, pursuant to an order of the Chief of the Main Staff, we were deployed by the commander of the Mostar city defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Let's look at the following document in the binder, which is P1615. This is a report that you submitted to the Military Police Administration, judging by the stamp, and you say in this report that on the 2nd and the 3rd --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wished to see whether this document was a follow-up to the previous document. Let me get back to the previous document. Mr. Stojic issues an order on the 7th of July in order to relocate a company of military policemen in Mostar. And then you said that you arrived in Mostar on the 30th of June, 1993. Why did you go to Mostar? What did you do there, exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We went to Mostar to reinforce units that were already deployed in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What did you need reinforcement for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, most probably there were not enough troops to man the separation line. We're talking one company only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say in order to be deployed. This wasn't aimed at providing a helping hand to those people who were disarming the HVO units in which there were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that was not the goal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When, on the 30th of June, you went to the unit of the military police, were there Muslims under your command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as you remember, where were you positioned, exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were billeted in the Herceg Stjepan Kosic Hall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is where you had assembled. But during the day, what were you doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What we did during the day? We were deployed on a front-line, and that's where we were, in shifts, manning that line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I thought that that was already clear and well known.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, on the 30th of June, what was the situation like in Mostar? Was your assistance needed because of the BiH attacks on the HVO units in Mostar? Did you know that? Was that the situation?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Madam, I know that there had been an attack of the BiH Army or that an attack was underway in the direction of Mostar and Citluk, with a view to taking Hum Hill and the surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, you're talking about the moment when you arrived? That was going on at the time when you arrived; right?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: There were attacks before our arrival, and some were ongoing at the moment of our arrival.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could we please look at P1615, which is the following document in my binder. I've already said that the document is your report, dated the 2nd of March, when some meat was stolen from the Heliodrom kitchen. Further on, it says that the head of the Defence Department called you, because you are the one who signed this report; right?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And he asked you about your observations of the Heliodrom facility. You carried out certain checks, and you informed Mr. Stojic that the military police was in charge of the main entrance into Heliodrom and that the other entrances are secured by other soldiers, and the head of the department agreed with your report. Mr. Andabak, are we talking about the entire Heliodrom barracks, the entire facility? Is that the main entrance that you had in mind when you wrote this report?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I meant. The military police control was weak at the main gate, and the military police was only at the main gate, not elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Which kitchen did the meat go missing from? Did you establish that when you carried out your observation task?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: The main kitchen which provided food for the troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, earlier on, to Judge Antonetti's questions, you talked about the arrest and bringing in members of the HVO of Muslim ethnicity, in 1993, in Livno. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber whether, in 1992, in Livno, whether there was a military prison there at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Madam, there was a military prison in Livno from the month of May to the beginning of September 1992. It was a prison which housed Serbs on whom weapons had been discovered.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And who provided security for that prison, Mr. Andabak? Who was it in the course of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: The military police, on the strength of the Livno Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And you say that the prison existed up to September 1992. And in 1993, was there a prison in Livno at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Madam, I would not say that there was a prison in 1993. I would say that it was more of a collection centre which existed as a place where disarmed Muslims were taken and stayed there from three to five days, depending on their role in their armed uprisal against Croats. And the body in charge was the brigade. The brigade military police provided security, and the staff of that brigade appointed by the brigade commander. In any case, the Active Service Military Police had nothing to do with incarcerated Bosniaks who were accommodated there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's look at P867 now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Andabak, I was still looking at the document on the theft of meat. You might say this was a minor occurrence, but we can see that an investigation was conducted, and from what I understand, you identified the perpetrators, i.e., the people that stole the meat. Strangely enough, I see the name of Mr. Tuta, who intervenes for Mate Culo to be released. Was Mate Culo one of the people who was suspected of having stolen the meat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me just clarify this. We didn't determined who had stolen the meat. But when I wrote this report, I talked to the operative duty office in the military police and said that I had another request from Mr. Tuta that we should release a certain soldier by the name of Mate Culo who was probably in the prison in Ljubuski, which was under the military police, and so I just let them know about that so that the Administration of the Military Police should know about this. And as I talked to Minister Bruno Stojic and sent this report, I sent in this request for release of this particular soldier, and I sent this out as a piece of information to the active-duty officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here is why I'm surprised: You report this to the minister of defence, Mr. Stojic, and you are reporting an incident with one soldier who is held, and you want this soldier to be freed. We don't really know what he's done. But why do you report this to the minister? Does that mean that at that time the minister of defence was following personally the situation of each and every soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, no, you misunderstood this. I am submitting this report to the operative duty officer in the Military Police Administration, whom I told that I had talked to the minister. I told the minister that I was in the location. I told him where the problem was about this stolen meat, and then I said that we would send in a request to have a soldier released. But we had no responsibility towards those soldiers or the prisons held by the brigade military police. So the defence minister had nothing to do with the release of prisoners, nor the military police. I'm just sending this piece of information about this request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Andabak, let's be precise. Your answer was that you were sending this report to the operative duty officer in the Military Police Administration, whom you were informing about your conversation with Mr. Stojic, and you were also sending him everything listed here?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, to the operative duty officer, and I informed the minister orally about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I see, thank you. You informed Mr. Stojic about the stolen meat, right, and the situation -- or, rather, what you established in that regard?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, and that's what it says in the report, what the military police should do, and the security, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Now look at P867, the next document, please. We'll go through that very quickly, because I've been informed that I only have 12 minutes left. Mr. Andabak, you were shown today document P781, which states the establishment of the -- the system, according to establishment, of the operative zone. And we see there that according to that organisation, we have the 2nd Military Police Battalion. And you answered a question from Judge Antonetti, saying that you were, with respect to document P781, subordinated to the commander of the operative zone in the performance of duties and tasks. And this document, signed by Mr. Siljeg on the 6th of December, 1992, it says: "On the basis of the arisen need and due to the formation of the Operative Zone of North-West Herzegovina, and with the aim of reducing the number of connections with the Main Staff, and in order to provide successful leading and commanding of the units, I order: "The commands of all the units of the HVO subordinated to the command of the Operative Zone of North-West Herzegovina, that they are obliged to send all requests and proposals and needs to the Defence Department through this command." Mr. Andabak, were you informed about this order, and did you act in conformity with this order?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: I was informed of this order at the briefing. And as you can see from the order, itself, we weren't named in this order, so we didn't have to act.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But you were informed of it, you knew about it?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now look at P1053.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: I don't seem to have that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It's document 3D, actually, 3D478, 3D478. Have you found it? The document is signed by Mr. Zrinko Tokic on the 22nd of January, 1993. And during the examination-in-chief today, you were asked about this document, or, rather, about document P1083, and your stay in Gornji Vakuf in January 1993. So this an operative report. Let's look at the last sentence. It says: "Units of this brigade," and we're talking about the Ante Starcevic Brigade from Gornji Vakuf, "and units added are co-ordinated and shall carry out all the orders issued by this command." Now, Mr. Andabak, this observation, does it refer to your unit as well, since at the time you were in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, this order does refer to the military police units, because they were under the command of the Ante Starcevic Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Once more, for the record, it was document 3D478. Yes, it's correctly recorded in the transcript. Now, Mr. Andabak, you spoke about Mr. Franjic today. You testified about him and said that sometime at the end of November, in an operation, he was arrested because of his acts -- because of acts committed in the Prozor area. Look at P6734 now, please. This is an order dated the 19th of November, 1993, in the which, under item 1, it says: "On the basis of military police security tasks at the Prozor-Vakuf front ..." The order is signed by Mr. Rade Lavric. And to go back to item 1, it says that the perpetrators of crimes were Andrijo Beljo, Ilija Franjic, and Ante Bradic, nicknamed Banja Luka [as interpreted]. These persons and all others responsible for the disturbing public law and order are to be arrested and taken to the Ljubuski Military Remand Prison. So was that the order under which Mr. Ilija Franjic was arrested?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Madam, that is the order, and that is the operation by which the military police arrested these persons and others who worked in cohort with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I missed a document. Would you look at 5D4377, please. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief today, you said that it was the commander of the Operative Zone of North-West Herzegovina that you received oral and written orders. Here we have one such order, where it says: "Pursuant to an oral order of the North-West Herzegovina OZ commander, Colonel Zeljko Siljeg, dated the 18 of April, 1993, I hereby order: "That one company from the active-service strength of the 2nd Military Police Battalion report to the OZ --" or, rather, "IZM, the forward command post at Prozor, by 0700 hours," report to Mr. Colonel Siljeg, "on the 19th of April." And we see that Mr. Ante Govorusic's name is written down there. Now, Mr. Andabak, did you receive this order and did you act upon it?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: I'm familiar with this order. We did receive this order. The Livno and -- and we sent to the Livno and Tomislavgrad unit reinforcements. And as for Ante Govorusic, somebody else signed for him:

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Andabak. My time is up. I'm told that was my last question. Thank you for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning [as interpreted], Witness. And, Your Honours, we have 20 minutes left, as I see, and I'll try and cover one area by that time. Could the usher help me out and distribute the documents, please. Your Honours, we also have 32 minutes, pursuant to your ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening, Witness. I am from the Praljak Defence, and I have a few questions for you. From your testimony and the documents we have looked at, and also from other exhibits and evidence that we have heard presented during this trial -- could I ask the usher at this point to hand over a set of documents to my colleague behind me. We seem to be concerned about the documents. And could -- I hope you're not going to count this time used up in the distribution of documents against me. So from your testimony and from other evidence presented here, I'd like to summarise certain facts, or, rather, I'm going to give you an observation. Tell me if it's correct or not. There are basically three forms of action of the regional military police battalions. The first is regional military police battalions act in conformity with the basic establishment documents governing the organisation of the military police; that is to say, they carry out their regular duties or typically military police assignments; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: That is correct, except the regional military police, that term you used, is not the right term. I don't know what you mean when you say "regional military police."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You're quite right. It's a technical term used frequently by people when they were talking about a military police battalion of the kind in which you were commander, because they were distributed in regions; right?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Secondly, the second form, which is exceptional, is that military police units sometimes carry out certain tasks and assignments of a military nature, just like any other typical HVO military units, and such assignments, in such cases, they carry out completely independently as a separately-issued order or assignment. Are there any such cases?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: I don't remember any cases where they acted independently. That's not right. They were always attached to one of the units, and they came within the composition of one of the units that already existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's try and clarify this and see what the documents say. Look at P05478 first, please. It's the first document in that binder. As we can see, it's an order signed by Mr. Valentin Coric, dated the 29th of September, 1993. It says: "Send the order urgently," et cetera, "to the 2nd Light Assault Battalion." But I'm interested in the last paragraph. It says: "Equip the unit with the requisite ammunition and equipment to permit them to operate independently in the utilisation zone to which they are assigned." And the dead-line for completion is such and such. So is this an independent assignment of some kind or is it an assignment which you will be given in more precise terms when you report to Siljeg, as it says in the first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Counsel, this unit is on the Mostar front. The unit, pursuant to a command from the Main Staff, is sent to the North-West Herzegovina Operative Zone to carry out the assignments and to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly slow down, please, thank you, for the benefit of one and all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They need ammunition and equipment, whether for RPG shells or whatever, and that's why Mr. Valentin Coric says that the unit should be equipped as if it was going to carry out an operation independently. And when it reports to the operative zone, then Colonel Siljeg will deploy it, deploy the men.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So we've explained this, have we?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether the witness is aware of this. Witness, the interpreters have complained that you speak too fast, and they ask you to slow down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's my fault, Your Honour, because we were speaking the same language and I wanted to speed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: From what you've told us, the independent action only refers to equipping the unit for it to be able to act when it gets to the area to which it has been assigned?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, so that it would be ready to carry out its assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When it is on loan to the unit, right, attached to it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's see whether the situation is the same with the next document. P1053 is the number. We've already seen the document today, but I'm interested in something else contained in the document. The document is dated the 5th of January, 1993, once again signed by the chief, Mr. Valentin Coric, and I'm interested in the last sentence there, which reads as follows: "These units are under the command of the chief of the Military Police Administration --" rather, "the commander of the 2nd Military Police Battalion located at the forward command post in Gornji Vakuf municipality." Now, tell us, what is being established here? Does this mean that you were within the hierarchy of the military police alone in your assignment, and were independent in that sense, or were you subordinated to some other unit on that assignment? Can you explain that to me, please?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Counsel, as we are dealing with the first active-duty military police --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. I think I misspoke. It's an interim report, but it explains something that was contained in a previous order. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: Well, here the chief of the Military Police Administration is informing the minister about this assignment, about sending men for the 1st Active-Duty Military Police Battalion, which was under the direct command of the Military Police Administration, and that is why it says that. That is why there is a separate order, because it was being sent by the chief, and the chief can send it to any locality under the command of the operative zone. But since I was in the operative zone already, they would report to me, and then through the command of the operative zone I would be given assignments for myself and for the active-duty battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So that is, once again, a form of re-subordination, right, but a little different in technical terms in this case; right?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO ANDABAK
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And this brings us to this third form. So the second was re-subordination. Once again, we've clarified that. Now, the third way in which this was done is as follows, and please correct me if I'm wrong --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The dates are very important for these documents, and this document is dated 5th of January, 1993. Colonel, according to the Prosecutor, the HVO issued an ultimatum on the 5th of January towards the ABiH, and I look at this document through the case of the Prosecution. This document is addressed to Mr. Stojic, and it's actually relevant to you because you have received some instructions. You were told to deploy your police units in Bugojno, Prozor, Gornji Vakuf, and Jablanica. 120 policemen of the 2nd Battalion and 35 policemen from the active battalion are actually involved in this operation. What is the purpose? Well, it's to preserve law and order and protect civilians. So according to you, is it an operation of an exceptional nature? Because we have the involvement of the minister of defence, Mr. Coric, as well as yourself, and we are dealing with four towns that are rather substantial. So what is the situation on the 5th of January which will trigger such a deployment of the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll tell you exactly what happened on the ground. You're just looking at the date, the 5th of January, but you're not looking at what happened a week before that and what the troop movements were; was it the BH Army or the HVO on the territory mentioned, and so on. In Gornji Vakuf, Bugojno, Jablanica, I had my platoons and companies, military police platoons and companies, which acted attached with the municipal brigades. And I spent time in those areas myself, and I saw the BH Army and how much they were bringing into the Gornji Vakuf area units from Zenica, for example, Fojnica, Travnik, and even, in part, from Bugojno. And I know for certain that the military police from Jablanica was already in some villages around Gornji Vakuf. I also know that the brigade commander had daily contacts with the brigade which was stationed in Gornji Vakuf; of the BH Army, I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I'm to understand correctly from what you've just said, this document should be interpreted given what happened the week before the 5th of January, when the ABiH launched an important action which led to the reaction from the military police from the HVO; is that what you're saying here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not what I'm saying. Every day in the past week, the BH Army forces infiltrated into these areas, and I found it necessary to inform the head of the Military Police Administration about the difficult situation in these municipalities. And, therefore, I was given instructions about what I should do under the circumstances. And as you can see, we have this interim report, and according to that, the first and prime task was to maintain law and order, and to protect the population, and to ensure that the roads were open to traffic, roads between Jablanica, Prozor, Vakuf, and Bugojno, in co-operation with the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding the last paragraph, and we will conclude with this question, is there not a contradiction with what you've just said? You said that the military police was subordinated to the brigade commander, but here you can see, in the last paragraph, it says that those units are under the command of the chief of the Military Police Administration; namely, under the command of Mr. Coric. Is there not a contradiction here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see any contradiction there, Your Honour. What I am saying is that in the establishment of the military police, the 1st Active-Duty Military Police Battalion was directly linked with the head of the Military Police Administration, and he can distribute them to any zone. And I was in OZ North-West Herzegovina, and I was at the forward command post, as it says, in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you're saying that, in fact, it's the 1st Active-Duty Military Police Battalion who was directly linked or under the direct command of Mr. Coric. As far as you are concerned, you are at the forward command post of Gornji Vakuf. Is that how I should understand what you said, or am I being mistaken here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're having trouble with the interpretation channels. The witness was receiving the English and not the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. When you answered my question, Witness, there was no interpretation, apparently. Could you perhaps repeat what you said when answering my question, my last question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I said was, Your Honour, that the Active-Duty Military Police Battalion had contacts with the chief of the Military Police Administration. But when they came to me at the forward command post, where I was, it was placed under the command of the operative zone, and I was there to co-ordinate them, how they should be taken in, deployed, and so on. So that's what this report refers to. The 1st Active-Duty Military Police Battalion could not come to the OZ without an order because it was coming in from another operative zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's on the transcript. It's 7.00. Mr. Kovacic, you will have 24 minutes left. You have had 8 minutes so far. We shall resume on Wednesday, at quarter past 2.00. Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Good afternoon. I just want to do make a correction to the transcript, which is no longer on the screen, but on page 89, line 15 and 16, when you asked the question, President Antonetti: "You referred to an ultimatum on the 5th of January towards the ABiH ..." And it may have been a translation error, but I think that should have been the 15th of January, rather than the 5th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: It should be the 15th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we may correct that. Probably the word "ultimatum," which somehow gets into the transcript, is wrong, but the question was about 5th January because the document is about 5th January, and that is why Judge started with "5th January"; am I right, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, the ultimatum could have been dated the 5th of January, not the 15th. The witness answered the question, whatever the case may be, and said there were other reasons for that. We shall reconvene on Wednesday at a quarter past 2.00 [as interpreted]. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 17th day of March, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.
